entries.title: Evil regex shapes (OWASP ReDoS)
entries.body: OWASP defines an 'Evil Regex' as one containing: a grouping with repetition, inside which there is (a) repetition or (b) alternation with overlap. Canonical examples: (a+)+, ([a-zA-Z]+)*, (a|aa)+, (a|a?)+, (.*a){20}. Against crafted input (a long run of the repeated char followed by a non-matching char, e.g. 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!'), the backtracking engine tries an exponential number of ways to partition the string before failing. A single such pattern on a hot path is a denial-of-service primitive.

entries.title: Catastrophic backtracking explained (regular-expressions.info)
entries.body: regular-expressions.info explains that backtracking engines explore every path through the NFA before declaring failure. When a repeated group is itself repeatable, or an alternation's branches overlap, the number of paths grows exponentially with input length, turning a 30-char string into billions of steps. The fix is to give the engine a single way to match each character: rewrite (a+)+ as a+ with surrounding anchors, or use atomic groups/possessive quantifiers where the engine supports them.

entries.title: Cloudflare 27-minute global outage (2019-07-02)
entries.body: Cloudflare's WAF shipped a managed rule whose regex contained catastrophic backtracking (the sub-pattern .*?=?.* effectively). Against request bodies without the expected delimiter, PCRE backtracked on every HTTP request across every edge server, pinning all CPU cores to 100% and taking a large fraction of the internet down for 27 minutes. The post-mortem identifies the backtracking regex as the root cause — the canonical proof that ReDoS is a systemic, not app-level, risk.

entries.title: Linear-time engines as the primary mitigation (RE2 / Rust regex)
entries.body: The most robust ReDoS defense is to run untrusted input through a non-backtracking engine: Google RE2 (C++), Go's regexp (RE2-backed), or the Rust `regex` crate. These compile to DFAs/NFAs that guarantee linear time and cannot be made to exponential-blow up, regardless of pattern shape. Where a backtracking engine is mandatory (JS/Python/PCRE), combine it with input-length bounds, atomic groups, and a match timeout.

entries.title: Atomic groups & possessive quantifiers (backtracking-engine mitigation)
entries.body: On PCRE/Java/.NET you can prevent backtracking into a sub-expression with atomic groups (?>...) or possessive quantifiers (a*+, a++), which 'lock in' a match once made. This neutralizes the ambiguous partition paths that cause catastrophic backtracking. JavaScript and Python `re` do NOT support these, so for those engines prefer pattern rewrites (single match path) plus a hard input-length cap as defense in depth.
